newsitem.title: USA: Money growth creates inflation - St Louis Fed's Melzer.
newsitem.headline: Money growth creates inflation - St Louis Fed's Melzer.

text.p: Rapid money growth -- and not economic growth -- is responsible for inflation, Louis Melzer, president of the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis, said on Wednesday.
"I want to stress that economic growth does not cause inflation," Melzer told an Arkansas State Bank Department's conference in Hot Springs, Ark., in a speech made available in New York.
"Persistently high rates of money growth, however you define them, translate into persistently high rates of inflation," Melzer said.
He said persistent inflation arises when the "prices of goods and services can all rise at once if the amount of currency in circulation is expanded enough.
"Thus, (the) monetary system can produce inflation. This is the basis for the assertion that inflation is a monetary phenomenon."

While admitting that price spikes can temporarily affect the economy, Melzer stressed that "temporary inflation is by its very definition less of a concern to monetary policy-makers. If it is temporary, it will dissipate on its own accord and requires no policy action."
San Francisco Federal Reserve Bank President Robert Parry said Tuesday that some of the forces holding prices down, such as workers' job insecurity and a strong dollar, may be temporary.

Melzer said the United States was "lucky ... to have had inflation of around 3.0 percent for nearly the whole of the current expansion. But this 3.0 percent is an entrenched, monetarily induced inflation which is not going to go away unless the Fed takes specific action to eliminate it," he stressed.

On March 25, the Fed raised the Fed funds rate, the rate banks charge each other for overnight loans, to 5.5 percent from 5.25 percent. It was the first rate hike in more than two years. But at the May 19 meeting of its policy-making Federal Open Market Committee, it left rates unchanged. The FOMC next meets in early July.

Echoing a defence of the Fed's pre-emptive policy that Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan presented last month, Melzer admitted "Of course, taking action to move the monetary inflation rate lower is controversial."
Responding to what he called "many of the Fed's critics ... that the Fed has been excessively concerned about inflation during the current expansion," Melzer said: "They are missing the point.

"The more successful policy involves watching inflation trends carefully and acting preemptively to stave off incipient inflationary pressures," he said. "The success of the Federal Open Market Committee's policy has been that the Fed has moved with enough agility to keep inflation at bay."
